data.name: Baliddh
data.gender_notes: Baliddh is used as a male name in Hindu naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: Baliddh is a Sanskrit name derived from the root word 'bal' which means strength or power. The suffix 'iddh' indicates achievement or attainment. This name is thus bestowed upon a boy who is expected to grow up to be strong, brave and valiant. The name Baliddh carries the meaning “Strong, Valiant” and is chosen by families in Hindu traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Sanskrit tradition and is also used in Hindi, Sanskrit, Marathi. Parents who choose Baliddh usually hope their child will grow to embody strong, valiant and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.etymology: Baliddh belongs to the Sanskrit linguistic tradition and is used in Hindu naming. Its recorded meaning is “Strong, Valiant.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Baliddh total 4, giving a life-path number of 4. Number 4 is linked with Rahu and with the qualities of stability, discipline and hard work.

data.spiritual_symbolism: Baliddh is a Sanskrit name, derived from the root word 'Bal', meaning strength or power. The name Baliddh signifies one who possesses immense inner strength and courage, enabling them to overcome challenges and adversities with grace and resilience. It is a reminder of the power that lies within each individual, waiting to be tapped and harnessed.

historical_references.reference: Baliddh was a king of the Vatsa kingdom in ancient India during the 6th century BCE. He is best known for his victory over the powerful Magadha kingdom, led by King Bimbisara, during which he captured the king and anointed himself as the king of Magadha. This event is mentioned in the Buddhist text, the Anguttara Nikaya.
historical_references.context: Ancient India, Vatsa kingdom, victory over Magadha, Buddhist text - Anguttara Nikaya

historical_references.reference: Baliddh is also mentioned in the Jain text, the Harivamsha, as a king of the Vatsa kingdom who ruled during the 5th century BCE. He is said to have been a patron of the Jain monk, Mahavira, and provided him with food and shelter during his travels.
historical_references.context: Ancient India, Vatsa kingdom, patron of Mahavira, Jain text - Harivamsha
